FR-H1: partly built: delivery builds main's exact revision (a detached checkout at that hash; the release, its artifact and the running product all name it), and a builder cell's change reaches main only through a passed gate, so a change its gate refused stays on its cell branch and is never built (FR-H1-AC-1); not built: delivery does not itself check that the revision it builds is one a gate passed. Main also moves without a gate: the kernel commits contract amendments and recompiled surfaces to it (kernel/compile.py update_repo_contract, update_repo_surface), a person's accept-as-is merges an unwarranted revision by design, and a commit pushed straight to the product repository's main is delivered (tests/test_deliver.py's commit_routes relies on it). Nor does delivery re-run the evidence: the product's test suite, the trace and fail-first are not run again on the built revision, only smoke checks and holdouts against the deployed product. It would take a build step that looks up the passed gate for the revision in the ledger, refuses one without it, and runs the gate's tests signal on the build checkout before deploying.
FR-H2: partly built: a release's record names its product and contract revisions, its requirement ids, the road rules it deployed under and every card it waited on with the person who decided it (FR-H2-AC-1); its capability pack pins the same revisions with each criterion's evidence state and the autonomy cap (FR-H2-AC-2); the evidence for a gate-proved criterion names the gate and the merged revision, whose ledger record names the policy that permitted the merge (FR-H2-AC-3); not built: none of it is signed. The pack says "not signed: no signer configured", and there is no signer, no key custody and no signature check. The links are also spread over the release record, the pack and the ledger rather than one provenance statement (an in-toto or SLSA style attestation) that a signer could sign and a verifier could check.
FR-H5: partly built: when a promotion fails in production, the factory restores the last promoted release there with no person involved, records the rollback and opens an incident (FR-H5-AC-1); a rollback keeps production's data (the current slot's data folder, or its volume on docker), so rolling code back never rolls data back, even data written under the newer release (FR-H5-AC-2); not built: there is no reconciler. Nothing compares what runs in production with the approved release and puts it back: operate.tick only probes production and opens an incident when a probe fails, so a process that dies or a slot changed by hand stays that way until a person acts. It would take a loop that reads the last approved release's package for each environment, compares it with the running slot (revision and health), redeploys the approved package when they differ and records each correction.
FR-H6: partly built: the ledger pins each release's product and contract revisions in its hash chain, and the product repository holds the code, its Dockerfile, its contract and its own standard-library test suite, so a copy of the repository and the ledger alone rebuild a release to the same tree and rerun its tests with the kernel not importable (FR-H6-AC-1), and the chain recomputes with sha256 over canonical JSON, catching an edited pin (FR-H6-AC-2); not built: the factory ships no standalone rebuild-and-recheck tool (the recheck in tests/test_brief_h.py is an auditor's own script); holdout scenarios are run only by the kernel (kernel/operate.py) from the factory's holdout custody, which is not among what the recheck reads; a docker or Azure image is not reproducible bit for bit (the Dockerfile's base image is a tag, not a digest, and image ids are not compared); and the release record (releases/<n>.json) and capability pack are outside the hash chain.
